procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Deputy Custodian-General dated May 1, 1954, dismissing the petitioners' case after hearing the parties.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The petitioners moved the Custodian-General of Evacuee Property for revision under s. 27 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, being aggrieved by the cancellation of a proposal and order, allegedly passed without notice to them.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioners approached the Supreme Court under Article 32 of the Constitution, seeking enforcement of fundamental rights, after the Deputy Custodian-General dismissed their case and the Custodian-General of Evacuee Property likely did not provide relief.

issue.issue_text: Whether the interest of a quasi-permanent allottee constitutes 'property' within the meaning of Articles 19(1)(f), 31(1) or 31(2) of the Constitution of India.

law.law_text: For an interest to be considered 'property' under Article 19(1)(f), it must be capable of being acquired and disposed of through normal modes like sale, mortgage, gift, or will.
Article 31(2) protects against the 'taking possession' or 'acquisition' of property.
Article 31(1) protects against the deprivation of property 'without the authority of law'.

application.reasoning: The Court found that the interest of a quasi-permanent allottee did not meet the criteria for 'property' under Article 19(1)(f). This interest is created by a statutory grant to a specific class of persons and cannot be acquired by an ordinary citizen in a normal way. Likewise, the allottee cannot dispose of it through sale, mortgage, or will.

The Court determined that the terms 'taking possession' or 'acquisition' used in Article 31(2) were inappropriate and inapplicable to the specific bundle of rights that constitute a quasi-permanent allotment.

Regarding Article 31(1), the Court reasoned that even if the interest were considered property, its cancellation was not a deprivation 'without the authority of law'. The cancellation was an enforcement of a right of resumption that was an inherent incident of the allotment itself, carried out under the same law that created the right. Therefore, the action was authorized by law.

conclusion.conclusion_text: The Supreme Court held that the interest of a quasi-permanent allottee does not constitute 'property' within the meaning of Articles 19(1)(f), 31(1), or 31(2) of the Constitution. Accordingly, the orders cancelling the allotments could not amount to a violation of fundamental rights under those Articles.

issue.issue_text: Whether the cancellation of the quasi-permanent allotments amounted to a deprivation of property without the authority of law, thereby infringing Article 31(1) of the Constitution.

facts: These allotments were cancelled by the Custodian authorities under the provisions of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, and its associated rules.
law: For Article 31(1) of the Constitution to be infringed, there must be a deprivation of property, and that deprivation must be 'without the authority of law'.
application: The Court reasoned that the cancellation of the allotments was not a deprivation without the authority of law.
It found that the right of resumption or cancellation was an inherent 'incident' of the quasi-permanent allotment itself.
The cancellation was carried out by the Custodian authorities under the very same law that had created the petitioners' rights in the first place.
Therefore, the act of cancellation was the 'working out' of a right that was part of the legal framework governing the property, not an action taken in defiance of legal authority.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the claim, holding that the cancellation did not infringe Article 31(1). Since the power to cancel the allotment was an integral part of the law that created the allotment, the cancellation was done with the 'authority of law', not without it.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the interest of a quasi-permanent allottee constitutes 'property' within the meaning of Articles 19(1)(f), 31(1) or 31(2) of the Constitution of India.
appellant_arguments: Under the quasi-permanent allotment scheme, the allottee is entitled to a right to possession, and this right to possession is itself 'property'.
respondent_arguments: The text does not explicitly state the respondent's argument on this issue, but the court's rejection of the petitioner's claim implies the respondent argued that the rights were too conditional and subject to cancellation to be considered 'property' under the Constitution.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the cancellation of the quasi-permanent allotments amounted to a deprivation of property without the authority of law, thereby infringing Article 31(1) of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The cancellation of the allotments was a deprivation of property without the authority of law.
respondent_arguments: The cancellation was not a deprivation without the authority of law, as it was merely the 'working out of the right of resumption or cancellation which was one of the incidents of the property'.
The cancellation was carried out by the Custodian authorities under the very law that created the allotment rights (Central Act XXXI of 1950).

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The interest of a quasi-permanent allottee is not considered 'property' that attracts the protection of fundamental rights under the Constitution, as the incidents of such an allotment are entirely statutory and include the inherent power of cancellation by the Custodian.
obiter: The word 'property' as used in Article 31 (1) may have been intended to be understood in a wider sense, and deprivation of any individual right out of a bundle of rights constituting concrete property may be a deprivation of 'property' which would require the authority of law.

While the rights of a quasi-permanent allottee are not fundamental rights, they are important statutory rights entitled to protection by administrative authorities and courts against usurpation of jurisdiction or abuse of statutory powers.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The interest of a quasi-permanent allottee does not constitute 'property' within the meaning of Articles 19(1)(f), 31(1) or 31(2) of the Constitution. Furthermore, even assuming the interest was 'property', its cancellation was not a deprivation without the authority of law, because the cancellation was an enforcement of a right of resumption that was an inherent incident of the property itself, carried out under the very law that created the allotment rights.
legal_tests_applied: In order that Art. 31(1) may apply, it is not enough that there is 'deprivation' but it must also be deprivation without the authority of law.
why_appellant_lost: The interest of a quasi-permanent allottee does not constitute 'property' within the meaning of Arts. 19(1)(f), 31(1) or 31 (2) of the Constitution of India.
Even assuming that the bundle of rights constituting such an interest in land is 'property', what happened in this case is not deprivation of the property without the authority of law.
The cancellation was not an illegal usurpation of jurisdiction by the authorities concerned so as to constitute negation of the authority of law.
Even if the exercise of that authority can be made out to be wrong, it is still not open to question having regard to ss. 28 and 46 of Central Act XXXI of 1950.
why_respondent_won: The cancellation of the allotments was the working out of the right of resumption or cancellation which was one of the incidents of the property.
The cancellation by the Custodian authorities was under the very law which created those rights.
policy_considerations: In holding that quasi-permanent allotment does not carry with it a fundamental right to property under the Constitution we are not to be supposed as denying or weakening the scope of the rights of the allottee. These rights as recognised in the statutory rules are important and constitute the essential basis of a satisfactory rehabilitation and settlement of displaced land-holders. Until such time as these land-holders obtain sanads to the lands, these rights are entitled to zealous protection of the constituted authorities according to administrative rules and instructions binding on them, and of the courts by appropriate proceedings where there is usurpation of jurisdiction or abuse of exercise of statutory powers.
